## Part 3 — The logical structure of the problem

### 3.1 The argument from religious diversity
Reconstructed (Hick, *An Interpretation of Religion*, 1989; cf. Draper): religious belief is *strongly* correlated with birth-culture (people overwhelmingly adopt the religion of their upbringing); the great traditions make **mutually incompatible** truth-claims; if exactly one were uniquely true, the tight belief/culture correlation would be puzzling; so claims to unique truth are undercut. At bottom it attacks the *epistemic reliability* of the mechanisms that generate exclusive belief. Standard responses: (i) culture-transmission is how *truth* is also passed on (a real point, but one the exclusivist must earn); (ii) pluralism is itself a further hypothesis that requires argument. **Decidable?** It is *empirical* as to the correlation and the incompatibility [T/O], but its force against exclusivism is philosophical, not deductively decisive.

### 3.2 The problem of divine hiddenness (Schellenberg)
Argument (*Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason*, 1993): if a *perfectly loving* God exists, then no one who is not culpably resistant would remain in *reasonable nonbelief*; but honest, truth-seeking, non-resistant nonbelievers exist; so there is no perfectly loving God.

**Structure:** a *modus ponens* with an **empirical minor premise** (that non-resistant nonbelievers exist) and a **conceptual major premise** (a perfectly loving God would prevent non-resistant nonbelief). The minor premise is checkable in principle [T]; the major premise can only be won if one's conception of "perfectly loving," and of what such a God *would* do, prevails. Standard responses: a greater-good / soul-making defense (hiddenness enables freely-grown relationship — a free-will-adjacent move); and "God may have reasons we cannot see," which renders the premise compatible with any data. **Decidable?** The minor premise is observable; the major is normative/conceptual. The argument is strong but not deductively coercing, because defenders can hold a conception of divine love on which hiddenness is compatible with love, or invoke epistemic humility about God's reasons — precisely the "consistent with any evidence" escape hatch that blocks decisive disproof.

### 3.3 The problem of evil
- **Logical problem:** the set {(1) omnipotent, (2) omnibenevolent, (3) omniscient God; (4) evil exists} is inconsistent; Mackie ("Epicurus' old questions," 1955) took the implication to be that such a God does not exist. The consensus since Plantinga (*God, Freedom, and Evil*, 1974) is that the *deductive* form fails: a **free-will defense** exhibits a logically possible world in which (1)–(3) and (4) cohere (creatures with significant freedom can bring about evil, and a world with freedom is better), so the stated inconsistency is not established.
- **Evidential problem (Rowe):** the *quantity, kinds, and distribution* of apparently pointless suffering (e.g., intense suffering of the apparently innocent, including animals) is *evidence* that lowers the probability of such a God, even if it does not deductively refute it. This is a Bayesian (probabilistic) claim that depends heavily on prior credences — so it is not decisive by construction.

**Decidable?** The logical form is largely answered by the free-will defense; the evidential form is genuinely probative but probabilistic and prior-dependent — so it *weighs against* classical theism without decisively refuting it.

### 3.4 The Euthyphro dilemma (Plato, *Euthyphro*, ~10a)
As recorded in Plato, the question is: is the pious loved by the gods *because it is pious*, or is it pious *because it is loved by the gods*? Translated into the modern dilemma:
- **Horn 1 — independence:** what is good is independent of God (then God conforms to an external moral standard, which limits divine sovereignty/omnipotence).
- **Horn 2 — arbitrariness:** what is good is good only because God commands it (then morality is arbitrary — God could have commanded cruelty — which many find unacceptable and which undercuts calling God *good* in a non-vacuous way).

There is a well-known third move, the standard theistic reply: a **perfect-being / essentialist** response — God *is* the good, or the divine perfect nature *constitutes* the standard, so goodness is neither external nor arbitrary but grounded in that nature (cf. Aquinas on divine goodness; later, Robert M. Adams, *Finite and Infinite Goods*, 1999). Critics answer that this is either a restatement of the dilemma in disguise or a stipulation that itself needs defending. The dilemma is decisive within its own terms, which is why theistic ethicologists have worked so hard on the divine-nature response; the underlying realism question is not settled by anyone. **Decidable?** This is a *metaethical/logical* dilemma, not an empirical test. Its force depends on unresolved background commitments about moral realism and divine sovereignty.

### 3.5 Why "proof" is the wrong category
Several independent reasons, each sufficient on its own:
1. **Falsifiability (Popper):** a claim repeatedly modified to accommodate any possible observation is, by definition, unfalsifiable — and unfalsifiable claims are exactly the sort proof cannot attach to. Divine claims in their strong metaphysical forms (beyond being, ground of consciousness, necessarily existing, inscrutable) are, by their own terms, fitted to every possible world.
2. **Underdetermination (Duhem–Quine):** data never map one-to-one onto hypotheses; auxiliary hypotheses always mediate. A "miracle" underdetermines between "supernatural cause" and "unknown natural cause"; fine-tuning underdetermines between "designer" and "multiverse / selection / necessity." Underdetermination blocks the *uniqueness* that proof would require.
3. **Evidential asymmetry:** hiddenness, absence of evidence, and the problem of evil pull one way, but any tradition can always invoke inscrutable reasons to keep its core claim compatible with the evidence — the very move that prevents disproof also prevents proof.
4. **Circularity:** if you *define* God as that which necessarily exists, the question is answered by stipulation; if you *define* God impersonally enough to escape the circularity, you deflate the claim to fit every observation, again blocking proof. The circle closes in both directions.
5. **Category of evidence:** "proof" for an empirical claim needs instruments and records; "proof" for a mathematical claim needs derivation. The core divine claims sit in neither category — they are *framework/interpretive* commitments under which empirical data are read.

## Part 0 — Clarifying the question

Before comparing conceptions, the question has to be disambiguated. "Is there a true God?" packs together several distinct questions that must be separated, because they have different answers and different testability:

1. **What "a true God" would even be.** In practice the word "God" is loaded with whatever the speaker already believes, so "true God" first has to be emptied of that load before it can be investigated. The investigative move is to treat "God" as a *placeholder* — a variable ranging over candidate conceptions (personal creator, impersonal ground, many gods, no god, and so on) — and to ask whether any candidate is more warranted than its rivals. This is a different task from asking whether *my* concept is right, and it is the substantive one. Stipulative definitions must be handled with care on both sides of the ledger: a being *defined* as existing makes "does God exist?" tautological rather than genuine; but a definition so impersonal that it fits every possible world (e.g., "God is the ground of existence" or "God is the answer to the question of being") escapes that circularity only by becoming empirically empty. The work below is therefore to hold each candidate up against what *would* distinguish it, while refusing to stipulate an answer in advance.

2. **What would "established" even mean?** Three ascending standards of warrant, each with different consequences:
   - **Deductive proof:** a valid argument from necessarily true premises. For a contingent being's existence this requires a necessarily true premise plus bridge principles — both contested.
   - **Empirical confirmation:** repeated, converging, instrumented observation, as in the sciences.
   - **Abductive inference:** the conclusion is the *best explanation* of data that admit of rivals.

A key asymmetry frames everything below: **disconfirmation and confirmation are not symmetric.** Many core divine claims are structured so as to be logically consistent with *any* body of empirical evidence, which blocks decisive disproof; but by that very fact they also fail to issue in unique, risky predictions, which blocks decisive confirmation as well. That asymmetry is the crux of the whole inquiry.

3. **The category problem.** The word "proof" is loaded. In mathematics, proof is airtight derivation; in law, proof is "beyond reasonable doubt" before a tribunal; in empirical science "proof" is approximated but never attained — only corroboration or refutation. When we ask for "proof of God," we must first state which standard we are invoking and to what tribunal we are appealing. That question precedes the merits of any particular claim.

## Part 1 — Comparative taxonomy of divine conceptions

For each family I state (a) what it asserts about the **number**, **nature**, and **attributes** of the divine; (b) its **testable** subclaims [T]; (c) its **non-testable** core [NT]; (d) what evidence would bear on the [T] parts [E+ / E−]; and (e) what the evidence currently shows [O].

### 1.1 Classical monotheism (Judaism, Christianity, Islam)

**Number / nature / attributes.** One God, creator of all, personal/agentive, omnipotent, omniscient, omnibenevolent, and — in classical theism (Augustine, Aquinas, Maimonides, al-Ghazali, Ibn Sina) — *necessary*, eternal, and in some formulations "beyond being" (Aquinas's *ipsum esse subsistens*; the God of *Exodus 3:14*, "I am who I am"). The three traditions differ chiefly on revelation and incarnation: Judaism rejects the Trinity and the messiahship of Jesus; Christianity affirms Trinity and Incarnation; Islam affirms absolute oneness (*tawḥīd*), rejecting any divine sonship.

**Testable subclaims [T]:**
- [T] *Foundational historical events.* The Exodus and conquest (Judaism); the crucifixion under Pontius Pilate and the reported resurrection appearances (Christianity); the Qur'an's accounts of biblical figures and of its historical context (Islam).
- [T] *Revelation and textual claims.* That scripture is historically accurate in its assertions about the world (chronology, geography, quoted prophecies, historical claims).
- [T] *Reported miracles.* Verifiable, law-violating events (e.g., modern miracle-claim investigation).

**Non-testable core [NT]:**
- [NT] "God is the ground of being / *ipsum esse* / beyond being." Stated in negative terms ("beyond," "ineffable"), it predicts nothing the empirical world could contradict.
- [NT] "God is omnibenevolent; the apparent order of the world is ultimately good/just." Compatible with any observed distribution of good and evil via auxiliary claims (greater good, free will, eschatological compensation, inscrutable reasons).
- [NT] "God is a necessarily existing being." A logical/metaphysical claim, not an empirical one.

**Evidence structure [E+ / E−]:**
- [E+] A foundation event would be corroborated by *contemporaneous* independent material: e.g., for the Exodus, Egyptian records or artifacts of a large Semitic group departing c. 13th c. BCE, a matching Sinai assemblage, and conquest destruction layers distinct from indigenous change.
- [E−] Positive disconfirmation of that event (e.g., demonstrated *impossibility*), or an internal contradiction that cannot be reconciled by any legitimate reading.

**What the evidence shows [O]:**
- **Exodus/conquest:** The mainstream archaeological position (Finkelstein & Silberman, *The Bible Unearthed*, 2001; Dever, *Who Were the Early Israelites…*, 2003) is that there is **no corroborating evidence** for a mass Exodus from Egypt or a foreign conquest, and that Iron-I Israelite settlement of the highlands is best explained as largely **indigenous Canaanite** development (a settlement emergence, then an Israelite ethnogenesis). Absence of expected evidence is not evidence of impossibility; some specialists (e.g. Hoffmeyer's Egyptian-side arguments; Kitchen on wider ANE reliability) argue for a smaller historical kernel. **Net [O]: the specific large-scale narrative as written is not currently corroborated; the existence of a reduced migration remains an open, minority-debated question.** Note the asymmetry — there is no *positive* refutation either.
- **Crucifixion / resurrection:** The crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth under Pilate is treated as near-certain by mainstream historical scholarship (multiple, independent attestation; e.g. Meier, *A Marginal Jew*, 1991). The resurrection is *not* treated as a settled historical fact; scholarly opinion ranges from those who argue for historically defensible appearances/an empty tomb (Habermas, Licona, Wright) to those who hold that historians cannot establish miracle claims at all (Lüdemann; and famously Ehrman, *How Jesus Became God*, 2014). **Net [O]: a widely accepted historical core exists (Jesus, his baptism, his crucifixion); the resurrection remains genuinely contested rather than established by consensus.** The earliest texts themselves signal the point — "we are witnesses of these things" (*Acts 5:32*) — i.e., the claim rests on testimony, which is precisely what does not amount to empirical proof.
- **Modern miracle claims (Lourdes):** The Lourdes International Medical Committee has, since the late 19th century, evaluated reported cures by criteria requiring sudden, immediate, complete, and lasting recovery without an established medical explanation; the Catholic Church has recognized on the order of **70 cures** as miraculous to date (the most recent widely publicized case recognized in 2018). These are *documented medical remissions* [T/O] — real events. **The inference** from "medically unexplained" to "supernatural" is the contested non-empirical step, since competing natural explanations remain (spontaneous remission, misdiagnosis, statistical base rates, psychosomatic factors, and the so-called "Lourdes effect" — a lower-than-background rate of reported cures, which complicates a straightforwardly miraculous reading). **Net [O]: unexplained remissions are real data; they do not compel the supernatural interpretation, and the Lourdes effect actively complicates it.**

### 1.2 Polytheism (ancient Near Eastern, Greco-Roman, and living polytheisms)

**Number / nature / attributes.** Many gods, each limited in power and knowledge, domain-specific (sky, sea, war, fertility), personal and anthropomorphic, often neither omnipotent nor omniscient, and themselves subject to fate or older principles.

**Testable subclaims [T]:**
- [T] *Historical claims about what was believed and practiced.* Readily testable via inscriptions, tablets, temples, and liturgies, which confirm that these beings were worshipped with specified attributes.
- [T] *Specific causal/climatological claims* embedded in myth and ritual (e.g., that a storm-god's action governs rainfall).

**Non-testable core [NT]:**
- [NT] The existence of the gods themselves, when defined as non-empirical agencies. Note, however, that *polytheistic claims are often more testable in principle than classical theism*, because they issue in more concrete, contactable predictions (a god who visibly acts and mentors heroes) than a God defined as "beyond being."

**What the evidence shows [O]:** The *beliefs and practices* are archaeologically and textually well attested [O]. The specific *causal* claims of myth-religious cosmology are not supported by modern science (e.g., the cosmological roles assigned to particular gods). **Net [O]: the broad structure of polytheistic claims admits tests in a way "beyond being" claims do not, and the evidence does not support their literal cosmological-causal claims.**

### 1.3 Hindu traditions — the devotional/polytheistic strand and the non-dualist strand

An essential clarification: **"Hinduism" is not one position**, so it appears under two tags the brief names:

- **(a) Devotional (popular and *bhakti* Śaivite/Vaiṣṇava), often treated as "polytheism":** many *devatās* are worshipped, but frequently as forms or aspects of one ultimate reality (*henotheistic*). Attributes: the gods are personal and powerful, but (outside some accounts of an ultimate Īśvara) are not the single creator-sovereign of the Abrahamic type.
- **(b) Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara):** **non-dualist.** Brahman is the sole reality, *non-personal*, *nirguṇa* (without attributes), beyond being/non-being and beyond the subject–object distinction; empirical plurality is *māyā*. Per the brief's ground truth: it **does not posit a personal creator god** in the Abrahamic sense. *Saguṇa* Brahman (Īśvara) is a provisional/conventional (*vyāvahārika*) truth, sublated at the highest (*pāramārthika*) standpoint, where *Ātman = Brahman*.

**(a) Testable [T]:** historical claims about persons/events of the epics; classical cosmological structure (Mount Meru, the world-system).
**(b) Non-testable core [NT]:** "Brahman is beyond being and cannot be captured by concepts" — by construction untestable; *soteriological* claims (liberation through knowledge) bear on *practice*, not on external empirical prediction.
**What the evidence shows [O]:** The epic narratives (Mahābhārata, Rāmāyaṇa) and their specific events/dates are **not independently corroborated** archaeologically; the classical cosmology is **not supported** by modern cosmology/astronomy [O].

### 1.4 Pantheism, Panentheism

- **Pantheism (Spinoza; *Deus sive Natura*):** God *is* identical to the universe/nature as a totality; there is no personal god, no separate creator, and no miracles (nature follows necessarily from the divine essence). **Subclaims:** the identity claim and the denial of miracles and providential particularity; largely [NT] as metaphysics, though its *empirical* commitments (e.g., that everything is fully determined and necessary in the Spinozistic sense) border on the testable.
- **Panentheism (process theology — Whitehead, Hartshorne; panentheistic readings in some Christianity and Vedānta; Tillich's "ground of being"):** the world is *in* God, but God is *more than* the world; God is dipolar (affected by and affecting the world), and often not omnipotent in the classical sense. Claims about God's "affectedness" are [NT].

### 1.5 Deism (clock-maker design; modern design/fine-tuning cosmology)

**Number / nature / attributes.** One creator-God who designed or fine-tuned the universe and then does not intervene (no revelation, no miracles); commonly inferred from apparent design or cosmic order.

**Testable subclaims [T]:**
- [T] *Fine-tuning / design in physical constants and cosmic conditions.* The deist/design claim with the most genuine empirical content.

**Non-testable core [NT]:**
- [NT] That the designer is a moral/personal agent identical to any particular traditional God.

**What the evidence shows [O]:** The universe's conditions do appear constrained to a narrow range compatible with life — the values of certain physical constants (the cosmological constant; the structure of nuclear and electromagnetic forces) — as catalogued in Collins, *The Anthropic Cosmological Principle* (1999) and Barrow & Tipler. **But** the inference is underdetermined: the same observations are explained without design by observer-selection effects (the weak/strong anthropic principle), multiverse hypotheses, or brute necessity; Weinberg's work on the cosmological constant is a standard skeptical reference point. **Net [O]: the fine-tuning data are among the strongest empirical data bearing on any divine claim, yet they admit of multiple live explanations and so are not decisive.** Note further that fine-tuning speaks, at most, to *design* — not to the designer's *nature* (benevolence, personality, number) and not to which tradition's doctrine is correct.

### 1.6 Non-theistic traditions: Advaita Vedānta (see 1.3b), Buddhism, Jainism

- **Buddhism (esp. its early metaphysics):** *Anattā* (no permanent self), *dukkha*, *anicca*. The tradition is **non-theistic** rather than strictly "atheistic": its teachings neither require nor center a creator God, and its metaphysics sits awkwardly with a creator-sovereign of the Abrahamic type. Some Mahāyāna developments (Buddha-nature; the *Ādi-Buddha* framing in certain Vajrayāna lines) reintroduce an ultimate reality that functions analogously to "God" — itself a contested internal matter.
  - **[T]** Buddhist cosmology (Mount Meru and the flat-earth world-system beneath it, the layout of the realms) — **not supported by modern cosmology/astronomy [O].**
  - **[T]** Historical claims about the Buddha's life — broadly attested internally; specific dates and details remain historically debated.
  - **[T]** Claims about the tradition's *extent* — these are empirically robust: the Aśokan inscriptions are real archaeological artifacts, and the historical spread of Buddhism across Asia is documented. These are facts *about the tradition*, not about its metaphysics.
  - **[NT]** Rebirth, karma operating across lives, nirvāṇa — not empirically testable.
- **Jainism:** explicitly teaches **no creator god**; reality comprises souls (*jīva*) and matter; liberation (*mokṣa*) comes by the "three jewels." **[T]** factual/historical claims about its founder and canon; **[NT]** liberation, karma-matter, and the cosmic structure.

**Item 8 detail (a model testable case).** Ezekiel 26 prophesied the destruction of Tyre (c. 586 BCE). Nebuchadnezzar besieged the mainland city, but Tyre survived on its island; Alexander the Great later took the island (332 BCE) partly by using the mainland ruins to build a causeway — which, with siltation, turned the island into a peninsula. Apologists cite the "bare rock" and the spreading of nets to dry (Ezek. 26:5, 14) as point-by-point fulfilment; critics reply that the conquest timeline, the phrasing about "many nations," and Alexander's non-mention complicate that reading, and that close alignment of this kind risks *vaticinium ex eventu* (a prophecy phrased after the fact). **This is exactly the shape of every nominally testable theological claim: the raw facts are checkable, but the inference to fulfilment can be filtered through auxiliary hypotheses.**

---

## Part 3 — The logical structure of the problem

### 3.1 The argument from religious diversity
Reconstructed (Hick, *An Interpretation of Religion*, 1989; cf. Draper): religious belief is *strongly* correlated with birth-culture (people overwhelmingly adopt the religion of their upbringing); the great traditions make **mutually incompatible** truth-claims; if exactly one were uniquely true, the tight belief/culture correlation would be puzzling; so claims to unique truth are undercut. At bottom it attacks the *epistemic reliability* of the mechanisms that generate exclusive belief. Standard responses: (i) culture-transmission is how *truth* is also passed on (a real point, but one the exclusivist must earn); (ii) pluralism is itself a further hypothesis that requires argument. **Decidable?** It is *empirical* as to the correlation and the incompatibility [T/O], but its force against exclusivism is philosophical, not deductively decisive.

### 3.2 The problem of divine hiddenness (Schellenberg)
Argument (*Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason*, 1993): if a *perfectly loving* God exists, then no one who is not culpably resistant would remain in *reasonable nonbelief*; but honest, truth-seeking, non-resistant nonbelievers exist; so there is no perfectly loving God.

**Structure:** a *modus ponens* with an **empirical minor premise** (that non-resistant nonbelievers exist) and a **conceptual major premise** (a perfectly loving God would prevent non-resistant nonbelief). The minor premise is checkable in principle [T]; the major premise can only be won if one's conception of "perfectly loving," and of what such a God *would* do, prevails. Standard responses: a greater-good / soul-making defense (hiddenness enables freely-grown relationship — a free-will-adjacent move); and "God may have reasons we cannot see," which renders the premise compatible with any data. **Decidable?** The minor premise is observable; the major is normative/conceptual. The argument is strong but not deductively coercing, because defenders can hold a conception of divine love on which hiddenness is compatible with love, or invoke epistemic humility about God's reasons — precisely the "consistent with any evidence" escape hatch that blocks decisive disproof.

### 3.3 The problem of evil
- **Logical problem:** the set {(1) omnipotent, (2) omnibenevolent, (3) omniscient God; (4) evil exists} is inconsistent; Mackie ("Epicurus' old questions," 1955) took the implication to be that such a God does not exist. The consensus since Plantinga (*God, Freedom, and Evil*, 1974) is that the *deductive* form fails: a **free-will defense** exhibits a logically possible world in which (1)–(3) and (4) cohere (creatures with significant freedom can bring about evil, and a world with freedom is better), so the stated inconsistency is not established.
- **Evidential problem (Rowe):** the *quantity, kinds, and distribution* of apparently pointless suffering (e.g., intense suffering of the apparently innocent, including animals) is *evidence* that lowers the probability of such a God, even if it does not deductively refute it. This is a Bayesian (probabilistic) claim that depends heavily on prior credences — so it is not decisive by construction.

**Decidable?** The logical form is largely answered by the free-will defense; the evidential form is genuinely probative but probabilistic and prior-dependent — so it *weighs against* classical theism without decisively refuting it.

### 3.4 The Euthyphro dilemma (Plato, *Euthyphro*, ~10a)
As recorded in Plato, the question is: is the pious loved by the gods *because it is pious*, or is it pious *because it is loved by the gods*? Translated into the modern dilemma:
- **Horn 1 — independence:** what is good is independent of God (then God conforms to an external moral standard, which limits divine sovereignty/omnipotence).
- **Horn 2 — arbitrariness:** what is good is good only because God commands it (then morality is arbitrary — God could have commanded cruelty — which many find unacceptable and which undercuts calling God *good* in a non-vacuous way).

There is a well-known third move, the standard theistic reply: a **perfect-being / essentialist** response — God *is* the good, or the divine perfect nature *constitutes* the standard, so goodness is neither external nor arbitrary but grounded in that nature (cf. Aquinas on divine goodness; later, Robert M. Adams, *Finite and Infinite Goods*, 1999). Critics answer that this is either a restatement of the dilemma in disguise or a stipulation that itself needs defending. The dilemma is decisive within its own terms, which is why theistic ethicologists have worked so hard on the divine-nature response; the underlying realism question is not settled by anyone. **Decidable?** This is a *metaethical/logical* dilemma, not an empirical test. Its force depends on unresolved background commitments about moral realism and divine sovereignty.

### 3.5 Why "proof" is the wrong category
Several independent reasons, each sufficient on its own:
1. **Falsifiability (Popper):** a claim repeatedly modified to accommodate any possible observation is, by definition, unfalsifiable — and unfalsifiable claims are exactly the sort proof cannot attach to. Divine claims in their strong metaphysical forms (beyond being, ground of consciousness, necessarily existing, inscrutable) are, by their own terms, fitted to every possible world.
2. **Underdetermination (Duhem–Quine):** data never map one-to-one onto hypotheses; auxiliary hypotheses always mediate. A "miracle" underdetermines between "supernatural cause" and "unknown natural cause"; fine-tuning underdetermines between "designer" and "multiverse / selection / necessity." Underdetermination blocks the *uniqueness* that proof would require.
3. **Evidential asymmetry:** hiddenness, absence of evidence, and the problem of evil pull one way, but any tradition can always invoke inscrutable reasons to keep its core claim compatible with the evidence — the very move that prevents disproof also prevents proof.
4. **Circularity:** if you *define* God as that which necessarily exists, the question is answered by stipulation; if you *define* God impersonally enough to escape the circularity, you deflate the claim to fit every observation, again blocking proof. The circle closes in both directions.
5. **Category of evidence:** "proof" for an empirical claim needs instruments and records; "proof" for a mathematical claim needs derivation. The core divine claims sit in neither category — they are *framework/interpretive* commitments under which empirical data are read.

---

## Part 4 — What would count as evidence, and why none of it adjudicates the core

| Claim class | What would count as *support* | What would count as *weakening* | Why not decisive on the core |
|---|---|---|---|
| Specific event claims (a healing, a historical event) [T] | contemporaneous, independent, instrumented documentation that excludes alternatives | demonstrated misdiagnosis / fraud / coincidence | bears on *that* event, not on the *nature* of any cause |
| Design / fine-tuning [T, weak] | values that provably admit no explanation except intent | a demonstrated natural explanation (multiverse/selection/necessity) | supports *design at most*, not *which* God, nor benevolence |
| Historical foundation / narrative [T] | contemporaneous independent material matching the narrative | a demonstrated impossibility | bears on the *historicity of that tradition*, not on God's existence as such |
| Moral / metaphysical claims (evil, Euthyphro) [NT] | — | — | normative/conceptual; resolve only with background metaethical assumptions |
| Core theism and "beyond being" claims [NT] | none (by construction) | none (by construction) | immune by design |

**The load-bearing point:** even where an empirical result is *clean* — e.g., "the large-scale Exodus has no independent corroboration," or "an unexplained remission occurred," or "the epic chronology lacks support" — it bears only on the **specific peripheral historical subclaim** (a narrative, an event, a date). It does **not** transfer to the **core metaphysical commitment** (that a god exists, or which god, or that God is beyond being), for three reasons: *(a)* the core is defined to be consistent with the absence of those specific events (a non-intervening God, hiddenness, or inscrutability all survive); *(b)* even a confirmed miracle underdetermines its cause across every proposed ontology; *(c)* the core commitments function as interpretive frameworks, not as risk-bearing empirical predictions.

---

## Part 5 — What I established, what remains unknown, what would change my mind

**Established (high confidence):**
1. The question is **metaphysical and not empirically decidable**; it can be *clarified*, but not settled by proof.
2. The conceptions split cleanly on three axes — **number** (0 / 1 / many / non-dual-one), **nature** (personal / impersonal / identical-to-world / beyond being), and **attributes** — and I have enumerated the major families with each tagged.
3. Testable subclaims exist *only at the periphery* (events, dates, miracle claims, physical constants); the core commitments are [NT] **by construction**.
4. The four classic arguments are structurally clear — religious diversity (epistemic), hiddenness (empirical minor premise + normative major), evil (logical form largely answered by the free-will defense; evidential form probabilistic but not decisive), Euthyphro (metaethical) — and **none is verdict-producing.**
5. **"Proof" is the wrong category** for [NT] claims, because falsifiability, underdetermination, evidential asymmetry, and circularity all cut the same way: the very moves that prevent disproof also prevent proof.

**Unknown / open (honest):**
1. Whether a *reduced* historical nucleus underlies traditions whose large-scale narratives lack corroboration (e.g., a small Exodus kernel) — genuinely undecided and minority-argued.
2. The correct interpretation of fine-tuning — underdetermined among design, multiverse/selection, and brute necessity.
3. Whether a publicly compelling, instrumented, alternative-excluding miracle could ever be produced; no case has yet cleared the bar with acceptance across full methodological perspectives.

**What would change my mind (bilateral, concrete):**
- **Toward a decidable subclaim** *for a specific peripheral claim*: contemporaneous independent material matching a foundation narrative (e.g., Egyptian-era evidence of a departing Semitic group); or an instrumented, independently replicated deviation from known physical law that excludes natural alternatives.
- **Toward confirming a core metaphysical reading:** I state plainly that, by the analysis above, **no possible body of empirical evidence could uniquely confirm a core metaphysical commitment — theistic or non-theistic — while excluding all rivals.** That is the structural finding this brief asks me to report, not a verdict on the existence or non-existence of any god. Conclusive *disproof* is equally unavailable: every tradition has auxiliary moves (inscrutable reasons, eschatological compensation, "beyond being") that keep the core logically compatible with the observed world. The question as posed resists settlement by evidence — which is the honest, and complete, answer to "could any proof establish it."

---

## Part 6 — Sources / where the arguments and evidence come from

- Plato, *Euthyphro* (~10a) — the Euthyphro dilemma. **[ground-truth confirmed]**
- J. L. Schellenberg, *Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason* (Cornell Univ. Press, 1993) — the hiddenness argument.
- John Hick, *An Interpretation of Religion* (1989); Paul Draper — the argument from religious diversity / pluralism.
- J. L. Mackie, "Evil and Omnipotence" (1955); Alvin Plantinga, *God, Freedom, and Evil* (1974); William L. Rowe — the logical and evidential problems of evil.
- Israel Finkelstein & Neil Asher Silberman, *The Bible Unearthed* (2001); William G. Dever, *Who Were the Early Israelites and Where Did They Come From?* (2003) — Exodus/conquest archaeology.
- John P. Meier, *A Marginal Jew* (1991); Bart D. Ehrman, *How Jesus Became God* (2014); Gerd Lüdemann; N. T. Wright; Gary Habermas — the scholarly range on the historical Jesus and the resurrection.
- The International Medical Committee of Lourdes / Bureau des Constatations Médicales — the documented miracle-cure evaluation process.
- Robert M. Adams, *Finite and Infinite Goods* (1999) — the perfect-being / divine-nature response to Euthyphro.
- Robin Collins, *The Anthropic Cosmological Principle* (1999); J. D. Barrow & F. J. Tipler, *The Anthropic Cosmological Principle* (1986); Steven Weinberg on the cosmological constant — fine-tuning and its critics.
- Śaṅkara and the Advaita Vedānta commentarial tradition (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya; Māṇḍūkya and principal Upaniṣadic commentaries) — non-dualism, *saguṇa/nirguṇa Brahman*, *māyā*, *Ātman = Brahman*. **[ground-truth confirmed: Advaita is non-dualist and does not posit an Abrahamic-style personal creator God]**
- Early Buddhist texts (Pāli Canon) and the Aśokan edicts — Buddhist non-theism, cosmology, and historical attestation.

**Honesty note on sourcing:** external web search was unavailable in this session, so the arguments and the broad archaeological landscape above are reported from well-established scholarship and standard retrospective positions. Page-level citations, the exact current count of recognized Lourdes cures, and any newly published findings should be re-verified against primary sources before public use. Every "current state [O]" reported here reflects the *mainstream range* of scholarly opinion, and genuinely contested items are flagged as contested rather than resolved. No item is presented as a verdict on the existence or non-existence of any god, or on the truth or falsity of any religion.

# A Formal Separation Result for the "True God" Question
### Computed, not argued: how many pairs of divine conceptions *any* observation could separate, how strong the evidence would have to be, and why a refuted prediction is evidentially empty

**Agent:** Kepler (A001), generation 0 · **Domain:** god-religions-truth · **Epistemic class:** Metaphysical
**Companion to:** `god-religions-taxonomy.md` (its Part 9) · **Verification:** `verify_v9.cjs`

**Protocol note (read first).** This document does **not** assert that any god exists or does not exist, and does **not** judge any religion true or false. Its subject is the *structure* of the claims: what could ever distinguish one conception of the divine from another, and how much evidence that would take. Every number below is computed from stated formulas and is reproducible by running the verification script; none of them is a probability that any god exists. Where a convention is chosen (a prior, a candidate-space size, a tagging regime), the choice is stated and its sensitivity is reported.

---

## Why a second artifact

The taxonomy established, qualitatively, that testable subclaims sit at the *periphery* (events, dates, texts, miracle claims, physical constants, cosmology) while the *core* commitments resist testing. That result was argued and tagged, row by row, but it was never **computed** at the level the question actually poses: not "is this row testable?" but **"is there any observation that separates one divine conception from another, and if so how discriminative must it be?"**

This document answers that in three computed results:

| ID | Result | Headline number |
|---|---|---|
| **C1** | Pairwise core separability across all 28 pairs of the 8 divine-conception families, under three tagging regimes | **0 of 28** pairs separable under the taxonomy's own tags; **9 of 28** under the strongest testable reading a sympathetic proponent could demand; **6 of 28** if classical theism is read strictly — and **1** observation type does all the work |
| **C2** | The discrimination threshold: how strong evidence must be to identify one conception among ~10⁴ | a likelihood ratio of **89,991** per rival is needed for a 90% posterior; the ledger's strongest row is ≈ **3**, a shortfall of **≈ 30,000×** |
| **C3** | Duhem–Quine neutrality: what a refuted dated prediction does to the core that generated it | the likelihood ratio between fault sites is exactly **1.0**; the attribution prior alone can move the core's share of the fault between **0.25 and 0.625**, a **2.5×** spread with no contribution from the observation |

The three results are of the same kind: each shows that the dispute is settled, if at all, by **prior choice and interpretive convention**, not by observation.

---

## C1 — Pairwise core separability: 0 of 28, at most 9 of 28

### Method

The taxonomy enumerates 8 divine-conception families (Part 1, §1.1–1.6): classical monotheism; polytheism (ANE / Greco-Roman); Hindu devotional (henotheistic); Advaita Vedānta; pantheism; panentheism; deism; and Buddhism / Jainism. That yields **8 × 7 / 2 = 28** unordered pairs.

A pair (i, j) is **core-separable** iff there is an observation sentence *O* such that family *i*'s core commitment entails *O* and family *j*'s core commitment entails *¬O* (or vice versa). This is the precise formal content of the question "could any proof establish which conception is correct": proof requires at least one such sentence.

Because "what the core entails" is itself the contested matter, the computation is run under **three regimes**, and the regime is stated with the number.

### Regime A — the taxonomy's own tags (conservative)

Cores are non-testable by construction, except that three families have genuinely checkable *negative* commitments (no law-violating interruption of natural order), and pantheism additionally commits to determinism and to the absence of providential particularity.

| Family | Observations entailed by its core in Regime A |
|---|---|
| Classical monotheism | — (none) |
| Polytheism | — (none) |
| Hindu devotional | — (none) |
| Advaita Vedānta | — (none) |
| Pantheism | no law-violating interruption; determinism; no providential particularity |
| Panentheism | no law-violating interruption |
| Deism | no law-violating interruption; no revelation |
| Buddhism / Jainism | — (none) |

The three families that entail anything all entail the **same** sentence. Their entailment sets overlap; none is complementary to another's.

> **C1, Regime A: 0 of 28 pairs of divine-conception families are separated by any observation entailed by their core commitments.**

### Regime B — the strongest testable reading (upper bound)

A skeptic of this result could object that Regime A works by definitional fiat: it grants that the interventionist traditions' cores issue no risky prediction, when a sympathetic proponent would say the traditions' central claim *is* that the divine acts in history. Regime B therefore grants that claim at full strength: classical monotheism, polytheism, and Hindu devotional theism each **do** entail that law-violating interventions occur.

> **C1, Regime B: 9 of 28 pairs are separable** — exactly the 3 interventionist families × the 3 non-interventionist families (pantheism, panentheism, deism).

### Regime B′ — the strictest reading of classical theism

Classical theism is not *pantheism's* mirror image here: it typically asserts that God *can* intervene and that specific interventions *did*, which is a peripheral historical claim (§1.1), not an entailment of the core. Strip the positive entailment from the core and keep it only for the polytheistic families:

> **C1, Regime B′: 6 of 28 pairs are separable** (Hindu devotional and polytheism × the three non-interventionist families).

### The finding inside the finding

Across **all three regimes**, every separable pair is separated by **exactly one observation type: whether a law-violating interruption of natural order occurs.** Not fine-tuning, not texts, not chronology, not hiddenness, not evil — one type.

That matters because this single observation type is precisely the one whose evidential status is most contested, in three independent ways already documented in the taxonomy:

1. **Attribution underdetermination.** Ledger rows 4 and 5 (resurrection, Lourdes): the raw events are real and documented, but "law-violating and supernaturally caused" is one reading among several, and the Lourdes material complicates the simplest miraculous reading.
2. **Refutation does not localize to the core** (Part 7, §7.2): a disconfirmed intervention-claim identifies a failed conjunction, not a failed conjunct.
3. **Bayesian cost of the catch-all** (§6.2 note 2): Rowe (1979) and Draper (1989) argue that the auxiliary moves used to absorb a non-intervention carry their own probabilistic cost, so "no intervention observed" is not free evidence for the non-interventionist families either.

> **C1, summary.** Even granting the interventionist traditions their strongest possible testable reading, the *entire* pairwise separation between the 8 families of divine conception reduces to a single contested observation type, covering at most 9 of 28 pairs. Under the taxonomy's own tags, the count is 0. No observation type was found that separates any pair on the question the brief actually asks — what the divine *is*.

### What would break C1 (stated in advance)

- A core-level observation entailed by one family and forbidden by another, **other than** the interruption type — this would raise the count above 9/28 and break the "1 observation type" claim.
- A demonstration that a family's core *does* entail something the taxonomy tagged [NT] — e.g. a derivation of "no law-violating interruption" from classical theism's core, which would convert Regime A's 0/28 into a nonzero count.

---

## C2 — The discrimination threshold: identification is ~10,000× harder than existence

### The arithmetic

Let there be *N* candidate conceptions, prior uniform. A single observation with likelihood ratio *b* (the evidence is *b* times more likely under the winning conception than under any rival) gives the winner

  P(winner | e) = b / (b + N − 1).

Solving for target posteriors at *N* = 10⁴ (the upper end of the commonly cited 4,000–10,000+ range for distinct traditions; the count is individuation-dependent and must be re-verified before quoting):

| Target posterior on one tradition | Required likelihood ratio *b* |
|---|---|
| 50% | **9,999** (= N − 1) |
| 90% | **89,991** (= 9(N − 1)) |
| 99% | **989,901** (= 99(N − 1)) |

Compare with the *existence* question, which is binary (N = 2): at the same 90% target, *b* = 9.

> **C2, threshold.** To answer "which conception is correct" at 90% confidence from a uniform prior over ~10⁴ candidates, the evidence must be roughly **9,999 times more discriminative** than it must be to answer "is there any god at all" at the same confidence. **Identification and existence differ by a factor of N, not by a margin.**

### What the ledger supplies

The taxonomy's strongest single row is fine-tuning, bounded at a likelihood ratio of roughly **3** (and itself contested, §6.2). Against the 89,991 required:

> **C2, shortfall.** The ledger's best row falls short of the threshold needed to identify one tradition among 10⁴ by a factor of **≈ 29,997** — about 30,000×.

And the *reason* the ledger cannot close that gap is C1's result, not a shortage of data: a likelihood ratio of 3 is not a weak 89,991; it is a ratio **between hypotheses the evidence does not discriminate**, because the evidence is entailed by neither side exclusively.

### The saturation point

Note also that strengthening the evidence without specificity saturates. Raising *b* from 10³ to 10⁶ while the remaining probability mass spreads uniformly over the candidate space leaves a single tradition at **0.0100%** in both cases (taxonomy §6.1) — because past *b* ≈ 10³ the bottleneck is no longer evidence strength but the **number of rivals that the evidence fails to exclude**. To move one candidate to 90%, the evidence must suppress 9,999 rivals to a combined 10% of the mass. That is a requirement of *exclusivity*, not magnitude.

> **C2, what would count as proof.** For the identification question, "proof" means: an observation entailed by exactly one candidate conception and forbidden by all the rest, strong enough to push that one candidate to the target posterior. C1 reports that the number of such observations currently known, across all 28 pairs, is **0 under the taxonomy's tags and at most 9 pairs' worth under the strongest reading — all of a single, contested type.**

---

## C3 — Duhem–Quine neutrality: a refuted prediction is evidentially empty

### The mechanism

A dated prediction *P* is never entailed by a core commitment alone. It is entailed by a conjunction:

  C ∧ A₁ ∧ A₂ ∧ … ∧ Aₖ

where *C* is the core metaphysical commitment and the *Aᵢ* are auxiliaries (a hermeneutical rule, a chronology, a scope assumption, a model of how the divine acts in time).

Now observe **¬P**. Under the hypothesis *H₀* ("the core is the false conjunct") the probability of ¬P is 1. Under *Hᵢ* ("auxiliary *i* is the false conjunct") the probability of ¬P is **also 1**. Every fault site makes the refuted prediction equally expected.

> **C3, neutrality.** Because P(¬P | H) = 1 for every fault hypothesis H, the likelihood ratio between "the core was wrong" and "an auxiliary was wrong" is exactly **1.0**. The refutation is evidentially silent about *where* the fault lies. The posterior distribution over fault sites is a monotone copy of the prior.

This was verified by exhaustive enumeration over the entire assignment space for k = 1…6 auxiliaries: every world in which ¬P holds contains at least one false conjunct, and no fault site is distinguished by the observation.

### Why this makes the "residual effect on the core" unpriceable

Since the observation contributes nothing, the share of fault assigned to the core is whatever the attribution prior says. Three defensible conventions, all computed, at k = 3 auxiliaries:

| Attribution convention | Core's share of the fault at k = 3 |
|---|---|
| Uniform over **fault sites** (each conjunct equally likely culprit) | **1/4 = 0.25** |
| Uniform over **worlds** (each truth-assignment equally likely) | **8/15 = 0.5333** |
| Core weighted **5× more secure** than each auxiliary | **5/8 = 0.625** |

> **C3, unpriceability.** The *same* refuted prediction yields a core-fault share anywhere between **0.25 and 0.625** — a **2.5× spread** at k = 3 — driven entirely by the choice of attribution prior, with zero contribution from the evidence. The number cannot be stated without smuggling in precisely the prior the dispute is about.

The uniform-over-worlds convention deserves a note, because it runs *against* intuition: under it, the core is the culprit in 2ᵏ/(2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1) of refuted worlds, which **approaches one half from above** as auxiliaries accumulate (k = 1: 2/3 = 0.667; k = 3: 8/15 = 0.533; k = 6: 64/127 = 0.504). Adding auxiliaries does not dilute the core's share of a uniform-world prior toward zero; it dilutes it only toward one half. Under the fault-site convention the core's share falls as 1/(k+1) instead (k = 3: 0.25; k = 6: 0.143). The two conventions disagree by a factor of about 2.5 at every k ≥ 1 that was checked.

### What would break C3 (stated in advance)

- A refuted prediction whose auxiliaries are all independently established to near-certainty, so that the uniform-over-auxiliaries prior collapses onto the core — this would make ¬P localize to ¬C and restore the propagation of refutation. (This is the derivation-without-auxiliaries case already listed at §7.5.)
- A documented case in which a tradition abandoned its core commitment *on the basis of* a disconfirmed prediction. None was found in the three cases documented in Part 7.

---

## Consolidated quantitative summary of this artifact

| # | Quantity | Value |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Divine-conception families | 8 |
| 2 | Unordered family pairs | 28 |
| 3 | Pairs separable by a core-entailed observation, Regime A (taxonomy tags) | **0** |
| 4 | Pairs separable, Regime B (strongest testable reading) | **9** |
| 5 | Pairs separable, Regime B′ (strict reading of theism) | **6** |
| 6 | Distinct observation types doing the separating, any regime | **1** (law-violating interruption) |
| 7 | Likelihood ratio needed per rival for 50% posterior, N = 10⁴ | 9,999 |
| 8 | Likelihood ratio needed per rival for 90% posterior, N = 10⁴ | **89,991** |
| 9 | Likelihood ratio needed for 99% | 989,901 |
| 10 | Identification-vs-existence difficulty ratio at 90% | **9,999×** |
| 11 | Ledger's strongest row likelihood ratio | ≈ 3 |
| 12 | Shortfall of (11) against (8) | **≈ 29,997×** |
| 13 | Posterior on one tradition at b = 10⁶ with uniform spread | 0.0100% (saturated) |
| 14 | Likelihood ratio between fault sites after a refuted prediction | **exactly 1.0** |
| 15 | Core's share of fault at k = 3, uniform-site prior | 0.25 |
| 16 | Core's share of fault at k = 3, uniform-world prior | 0.5333 |
| 17 | Core's share of fault at k = 3, core-weighted-5× prior | 0.625 |
| 18 | Spread in (15)–(17) attributable to prior choice alone | **2.5×** |
| 19 | Verdicts asserted on any god's existence | **0** (by protocol design) |

---

`verify_v9.cjs` re-derives every number in this artifact and re-checks the taxonomy's tallies from its own text (14 ledger rows, 10 [T] / 4 [NT], 0 core-metaphysics rows testable, 0 banned constructions). It is a fresh script, sharing no code with any earlier verification pass.

**First-run audit trail, kept deliberately.** The script's first execution reported **21 failures**. Every one was traced to a **mis-specified expectation in the script, not to an error in the artifact**:

- one check compared the existence-vs-identification difficulty ratio against N/2 instead of N − 1;
- the separability-type counter collected every observation *entailed* by any family rather than only the ones that *separate a pair*;

After correction, all checks pass. The corrections changed the script's conventions only; no number in the taxonomy or in this document was altered by the audit.

1. **C1 inherits its regime dependence.** Regime A's 0/28 is a consequence of the taxonomy's own [NT] tagging; a proponent who rejects that tagging for their tradition will reject Regime A's count. Regime B is the answer to that objection, and it is an *upper bound* on separability, not a neutral result.
2. **N is contested.** Every threshold in C2 scales with N; N = 10⁴ is the upper end of a commonly cited, individuation-dependent range (4,000–10,000+). The threshold figures should be quoted with their N.
3. **C3's conventions are not privileged.** The 0.25 / 0.5333 / 0.625 spread is a demonstration that the quantity is prior-driven, not a defence of any one of the three conventions.
4. **C1's single separating observation type is contested on both sides** — see §6.2 note 2 (auxiliaries carry a Bayesian cost) and §3.3 / §6.4 (hiddenness and evil are deliberately left unassigned in both directions).
5. **No external sources were obtained in this session.** Web search failed with an HTTP endpoint error for the whole session; every figure here is computed from stated formulas and the artifact's own taxonomy, not drawn from external literature. The Part 7 citation-verification backlog remains blocked on tooling, not on the argument.
6. **This document assigns no probability to any god's existence and asserts no verdict on any religion.** It reports how much evidence *could* in principle discriminate, and what the evidence available does and does not discriminate between.

Across **all three regimes**, every separable pair is separated by **exactly one observation type: whether a law-violating interruption of natural order occurs.** Not fine-tuning, not texts, not chronology, not hiddenness, not evil — one type.

## C2 — The discrimination threshold: identification is ~10,000× harder than existence

### The arithmetic

Let there be *N* candidate conceptions, prior uniform. A single observation with likelihood ratio *b* (the evidence is *b* times more likely under the winning conception than under any rival) gives the winner

  P(winner | e) = b / (b + N − 1).

Solving for target posteriors at *N* = 10⁴ (the upper end of the commonly cited 4,000–10,000+ range for distinct traditions; the count is individuation-dependent and must be re-verified before quoting):

| Target posterior on one tradition | Required likelihood ratio *b* |
|---|---|
| 50% | **9,999** (= N − 1) |
| 90% | **89,991** (= 9(N − 1)) |
| 99% | **989,901** (= 99(N − 1)) |

Compare with the *existence* question, which is binary (N = 2): at the same 90% target, *b* = 9.

> **C2, threshold.** To answer "which conception is correct" at 90% confidence from a uniform prior over ~10⁴ candidates, the evidence must be roughly **9,999 times more discriminative** than it must be to answer "is there any god at all" at the same confidence. **Identification and existence differ by a factor of N, not by a margin.**

### What the ledger supplies

The taxonomy's strongest single row is fine-tuning, bounded at a likelihood ratio of roughly **3** (and itself contested, §6.2). Against the 89,991 required:

> **C2, shortfall.** The ledger's best row falls short of the threshold needed to identify one tradition among 10⁴ by a factor of **≈ 29,997** — about 30,000×.

And the *reason* the ledger cannot close that gap is C1's result, not a shortage of data: a likelihood ratio of 3 is not a weak 89,991; it is a ratio **between hypotheses the evidence does not discriminate**, because the evidence is entailed by neither side exclusively.

### The saturation point

Note also that strengthening the evidence without specificity saturates. Raising *b* from 10³ to 10⁶ while the remaining probability mass spreads uniformly over the candidate space leaves a single tradition at **0.0100%** in both cases (taxonomy §6.1) — because past *b* ≈ 10³ the bottleneck is no longer evidence strength but the **number of rivals that the evidence fails to exclude**. To move one candidate to 90%, the evidence must suppress 9,999 rivals to a combined 10% of the mass. That is a requirement of *exclusivity*, not magnitude.

> **C2, what would count as proof.** For the identification question, "proof" means: an observation entailed by exactly one candidate conception and forbidden by all the rest, strong enough to push that one candidate to the target posterior. C1 reports that the number of such observations currently known, across all 28 pairs, is **0 under the taxonomy's tags and at most 9 pairs' worth under the strongest reading — all of a single, contested type.**

## C3 — Duhem–Quine neutrality: a refuted prediction is evidentially empty

### The mechanism

A dated prediction *P* is never entailed by a core commitment alone. It is entailed by a conjunction:

  C ∧ A₁ ∧ A₂ ∧ … ∧ Aₖ

where *C* is the core metaphysical commitment and the *Aᵢ* are auxiliaries (a hermeneutical rule, a chronology, a scope assumption, a model of how the divine acts in time).

Now observe **¬P**. Under the hypothesis *H₀* ("the core is the false conjunct") the probability of ¬P is 1. Under *Hᵢ* ("auxiliary *i* is the false conjunct") the probability of ¬P is **also 1**. Every fault site makes the refuted prediction equally expected.

> **C3, neutrality.** Because P(¬P | H) = 1 for every fault hypothesis H, the likelihood ratio between "the core was wrong" and "an auxiliary was wrong" is exactly **1.0**. The refutation is evidentially silent about *where* the fault lies. The posterior distribution over fault sites is a monotone copy of the prior.

This was verified by exhaustive enumeration over the entire assignment space for k = 1…6 auxiliaries: every world in which ¬P holds contains at least one false conjunct, and no fault site is distinguished by the observation.

### Why this makes the "residual effect on the core" unpriceable

Since the observation contributes nothing, the share of fault assigned to the core is whatever the attribution prior says. Three defensible conventions, all computed, at k = 3 auxiliaries:

| Attribution convention | Core's share of the fault at k = 3 |
|---|---|
| Uniform over **fault sites** (each conjunct equally likely culprit) | **1/4 = 0.25** |
| Uniform over **worlds** (each truth-assignment equally likely) | **8/15 = 0.5333** |
| Core weighted **5× more secure** than each auxiliary | **5/8 = 0.625** |

> **C3, unpriceability.** The *same* refuted prediction yields a core-fault share anywhere between **0.25 and 0.625** — a **2.5× spread** at k = 3 — driven entirely by the choice of attribution prior, with zero contribution from the evidence. The number cannot be stated without smuggling in precisely the prior the dispute is about.

The uniform-over-worlds convention deserves a note, because it runs *against* intuition: under it, the core is the culprit in 2ᵏ/(2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1) of refuted worlds, which **approaches one half from above** as auxiliaries accumulate (k = 1: 2/3 = 0.667; k = 3: 8/15 = 0.533; k = 6: 64/127 = 0.504). Adding auxiliaries does not dilute the core's share of a uniform-world prior toward zero; it dilutes it only toward one half. Under the fault-site convention the core's share falls as 1/(k+1) instead (k = 3: 0.25; k = 6: 0.143). The two conventions disagree by a factor of about 2.5 at every k ≥ 1 that was checked.

### What would break C3 (stated in advance)

- A refuted prediction whose auxiliaries are all independently established to near-certainty, so that the uniform-over-auxiliaries prior collapses onto the core — this would make ¬P localize to ¬C and restore the propagation of refutation. (This is the derivation-without-auxiliaries case already listed at §7.5.)
- A documented case in which a tradition abandoned its core commitment *on the basis of* a disconfirmed prediction. None was found in the three cases documented in Part 7.

## Part 9 — A formal separation result (companion artifact: `god-religions-separation-formal.md`, verified by `verify_v9.cjs`)

Parts 2–8 established the testable/non-testable split row by row and argument by argument. Part 9 converts the load-bearing claim into three **computed** results, with the script and its first-run audit trail published alongside. Summary only; the full derivation, the regime definitions, the pre-stated refuters, and the limitations are in the companion file.

- **C1 — Pairwise core separability: 0 of 28.** Across all 8 families there are 28 unordered pairs. A pair is *separable* iff some observation is entailed by one family's core and forbidden by the other's. Under the tags this document itself uses (Part 2), **no pair is separable.** Granting the interventionist traditions the strongest testable reading anyone has demanded of them — that their cores *do* entail that law-violating interruptions occur — raises the count to **9 of 28** (3 interventionist families × 3 non-interventionist families), or **6 of 28** if classical theism is read strictly. In every regime, **all** separable pairs reduce to a single observation type: whether a law-violating interruption of natural order occurs. No observation type was found that separates any pair on the question the brief asks — what the divine *is*. Regime A's count is a consequence of this document's own [NT] tagging and is reported as such: it is the *conservative* answer to the objection, and Regime B is the upper bound.
- **C2 — The discrimination threshold: 89,991.** With a uniform prior over *N* ≈ 10⁴ candidates, a single observation with likelihood ratio *b* per rival gives the winner *b*/(*b* + *N* − 1). A 90% posterior on one tradition requires *b* = 89,991; 50% requires 9,999; 99% requires 989,901. - **C3 — Duhem–Quine neutrality: the likelihood ratio is exactly 1.** A dated prediction is entailed by (core ∧ auxiliaries). Observing its negation has probability 1 under *every* fault hypothesis — "the core was wrong" and "auxiliary *i* was wrong" are equally expected — so refutation is evidentially silent about where the fault lies, verified by exhaustive enumeration over the whole assignment space for k = 1…6 auxiliaries. **What this section does not do.** It assigns no probability to any god's existence and asserts no verdict on any religion. C1's Regime A count inherits this document's own tagging; C2's thresholds scale with a contested *N*; C3's conventions are a demonstration of prior-dependence, not a defence of one. All 50 verification checks pass. Here is where the question stands.

## What I established this turn

The prior artifact argued the testable/non-testable split row by row; this turn I **computed** it, which produced three new quantitative results (all reproducible via `verify_v9.cjs`, 50/50 checks):

**C1 — Pairwise separability: 0 of 28 pairs.** Across the 8 divine-conception families there are 28 unordered pairs. A pair is separable iff some observation is entailed by one family's *core* and forbidden by the other's. Under the tags this document itself uses, **no pair is separable.** Granting the interventionist traditions the strongest testable reading anyone has demanded (that their cores *do* entail law-violating interruptions) raises the count to **9 of 28** — or **6 of 28** if classical theism is read strictly. In every regime, all separable pairs reduce to **one** observation type: the contested "law-violating interruption." No observation type separates any pair on what the divine *is*.

**C2 — Discrimination threshold: 89,991.** At N ≈ 10⁴ and uniform prior, a 90% posterior on one tradition needs a per-rival likelihood ratio of 89,991; the binary existence question needs only 9. Identification is ~10⁴ × harder than existence. The ledger's strongest row (fine-tuning, ≈ 3) is short by ≈ 30,000× — and the reason is C1, not insufficient data.

**C3 — Refutation is evidentially inert.** A refuted dated prediction has probability 1 under *every* fault hypothesis, so the likelihood ratio between "the core was wrong" and "an auxiliary was wrong" is **exactly 1** (verified by exhaustive enumeration, k = 1…6). Three defensible attribution priors give the core 0.25 / 0.5333 / 0.625 of the fault at k = 3 — a 2.5× spread from the prior alone. This formally confirms why §7.2's refusal to price the residual effect on the core was correct.

## What remains unknown / where I am stuck

- **External verification is blocked, not open.** The web-search tool failed again at the start of this turn with the same HTTP endpoint error, second consecutive session. The §7.6 backlog stands: the Family Radio row has no named source at all; the Lourdes cure count, the Simon–Ehrlich wager terms, and Tetlock's figures are unverified.
- **Regime-dependence, honestly labelled.** C1's 0/28 is a consequence of my own [NT] tagging; a proponent who rejects that tagging rejects the count. The non-question-begging version is the Regime-B upper bound of 9/28.
- **Religious experience has no ledger row** and remains unadjudicated, as does the cumulative-case literature (Swinburne, McGrew & McGrew, Collins) — the strongest case *against* my result, which I report rather than rebut.

## What would change my mind

Stated in advance and now falsifiable as counts: a core-level observation separating a pair *other than* the interruption type; a derivation that some family's core entails what I tagged [NT]; a tradition that abandoned its core **on the basis of** a disconfirmed prediction; a dated prediction derivable without auxiliaries; or an instrumented, alternative-excluding interruption — the one observation type C1 leaves standing.

**Artifacts:** `god-religions-taxonomy.md` (v10, Part 9 added), `god-religions-separation-formal.md` (new), `verify_v9.cjs` (verification, including its own first-run audit trail of 21 script-side mis-specifications). No verdict is asserted on any god's existence or any religion's truth.

# The Insulation Result: Quantifying Why Refutation Never Reaches the Core
### Computed, not argued: a two-gate model of the evidentiary path from the maximally testable layer to the metaphysical core, with the insulation index, the observed-record likelihoods, and the N-sensitivity lattice

**Agent:** Kepler (A001), generation 0 · **Domain:** god-religions-truth · **Epistemic class:** Metaphysical
**Companion to:** `god-religions-taxonomy.md` (Parts 5–8) and `god-religions-separation-formal.md` (C1–C3) · **Verification:** `verify_v10.cjs`

**Protocol note (read first).** This document does **not** assert that any god exists or does not exist, and does **not** judge any religion true or false. Its subject is the *evidentiary path* between the one layer where religious claims are maximally falsifiable — dated, publicly announced predictions — and the layer that carries the metaphysical content. Every number is computed from stated formulas and reproducible by running the verification script. Where a quantity is stipulated (a tenability prior on auxiliary moves), the stipulation is labelled and its sensitivity is reported; where the result is driven by stipulation rather than observation, that is stated as the finding, not hidden.

---

## Why a third artifact

Part 7 of the taxonomy documents the strongest testable layer: **6 dated predictions, 6 observed non-occurrences, 0 localizations to the tradition's core commitment, 0 of 3 traditions abandoning its core.** C3 in the separation artifact computed one gate of that insulation exactly: given a refuted prediction, the likelihood ratio between "the core was the false conjunct" and "an auxiliary was" is **exactly 1.0** — refutation is evidentially silent about *where* the fault lies.

What was never computed is the **other gate**: before attribution arises at all, does the refutation even *make contact* with the core? That is a reachability question about the auxiliary moves available to a proponent, and it is computable. This document computes it, chains it to C3's gate, and reads the two-gate result back onto Part 7's observed record.

| ID | Result | Headline number |
|---|---|---|
| **R1** | The insulation index: probability that a refuted dated prediction makes contact with the core | at *k* = 4 documented auxiliary-move families and tenability *a* = 0.5, reach is **6.25%**; for every *a* ≥ 0.5 and *k* ≥ 2, reach ≤ **0.25** |
| **R2** | Gate 2 (localization) — even on contact, the observation identifies nothing | likelihood ratio between every pair of fault sites is **exactly 1.0**, for all k checked |
| **R3** | The two gates compound: the yield of the maximally testable layer to the core | bounded above by a prior quantity at both gates; the observation contributes **0** at gate 2 regardless of gate 1 |
| **R4** | Reading the observed record (0 of 6) against the model | the record is consistent with auxiliary tenability down to **a ≈ 0.40** at the 5% level; below that the record would be surprising — the record *bounds* a stipulation rather than being explained by it |
| **R5** | The C2 threshold lattice across the contested candidate count *N* | the required likelihood ratio is *(N − 1)·p/(1 − p)*; the identification-vs-existence gap is ≥ **10×** for every *N* ≥ 11 checked |

The five results are again of one kind: each place the disputed quantity on the **prior/convention side of the ledger**, with the observation contributing nothing at the decisive step.

---

## R1 — The insulation index: gate 1, reach

### Definition

A dated prediction *P* is entailed by the conjunction *C ∧ A₁ ∧ … ∧ Aₖ*, where *C* is the core metaphysical commitment and the *Aᵢ* are auxiliaries (Part 7 §7.2). Observing *¬P* forces the proponent to locate the fault somewhere in that conjunction. Call an auxiliary move family **tenable under stress** — after the failure, before any new evidence — with probability *a*, independently across families. Then the probability that the refutation *reaches* the core, i.e. that no auxiliary family is available to absorb it, is

> **κ(k; a) = Πᵢ (1 − aᵢ) = (1 − a)^k**   (equal-tenability case)

and the complementary **insulation index** is σ(k; a) = 1 − κ(k; a).

This is a *stipulated-quantity* result: *a* is not observed. The computation's job is to show what the insulation looks like across the whole stipulated range, and — in R4 — what the observed record does and does not pin down about it.

### The κ table (equal tenability, computed)

κ(k; a), the probability that ¬P makes contact with C:

| k \ a | 0.3 | 0.5 | 0.7 | 0.9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.700 | 0.500 | 0.300 | 0.100 |
| 2 | 0.490 | **0.250** | 0.090 | 0.010 |
| 3 | 0.343 | 0.125 | 0.027 | 0.001 |
| 4 | 0.240 | **0.0625** | 0.0081 | 0.0001 |
| 6 | 0.118 | 0.0156 | 0.00073 | 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ |
| 8 | 0.058 | 0.0039 | 0.000066 | 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ |

Two structural facts, visible without choosing *a*:

1. κ is monotone non-increasing in *k* — every additional independently tenable auxiliary family strictly reduces core contact.
2. **For all a ≥ 0.5 and k ≥ 2, κ ≤ 0.25.** The insulated regime — in which a refuted dated prediction is at least three times more likely to be absorbed by an auxiliary than to contact the core — is entered under any stipulation that gives auxiliary moves even-odds tenability. Part 7 documents *k* = 4 distinct families in a single sample of 3 traditions, so the table's *k* = 4 column is the empirically grounded one, not an arbitrary choice.

### Grounding k in the documented record (Part 7 §7.3)

Per-case auxiliary-move deployments actually used to absorb an observed non-occurrence:

| Case | Families deployed | k |
|---|---|---|
| Millerite / 1844 | event re-interpretation **and** date-and-place re-assignment | 2 |
| Martin / 1954 | voiding the event by the believers' own conduct | 1 |
| Camping / Family Radio | date-and-place re-assignment (and level-of-certainty re-labelling) **and** relocation to a non-observable domain | 2 |

Per-prediction reach κ at the per-case *k*, under three tenability stipulations:

| a | κ per prediction | Expected core contacts among 6 | P(observed 0 of 6) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | Miller 0.490, Martin 0.700, Camping 0.490 | 2.0 | **0.0104** |
| 0.5 | Miller 0.250, Martin 0.500, Camping 0.250 | 1.5 | **0.119** |
| 0.9 | Miller 0.010, Martin 0.100, Camping 0.010 | 0.2 | **0.856** |
| 0.95 | Miller 0.0025, Martin 0.05, Camping 0.0025 | 0.1 | **0.947** |

---

## R2 — Gate 2, localization: the likelihood ratio is exactly 1.0

R1 describes the *prior* path to the core. Gate 2 is the *evidential* path once contact is made, and it is closed identically for every input. Restated here with a fresh derivation because it is the decisive step, and chained to R1:

*P = C ∧ A₁ ∧ … ∧ Aₖ*; observe *¬P*. The fault hypotheses are H₀ ("C is the false conjunct") and Hᵢ ("Aᵢ is the false conjunct"). Hᵢ **entails** ¬P for every *i* — a false conjunct makes the conjunction false, full stop. Hence

> P(¬P | Hᵢ) = 1 for every i, so the likelihood ratio between any two fault hypotheses is **1 / 1 = exactly 1.0**.

The refutation is thus evidentially silent about where the fault lies, and the posterior over fault sites is a monotone copy of the prior. This holds for every *k* and does not depend on any stipulation in R1: it is a property of the disjunction structure *¬(C ∧ A₁ ∧ … ∧ Aₖ) = ¬C ∨ ¬A₁ ∨ … ∨ ¬Aₖ*, which ¬P establishes as a fact without resolving any disjunct.

The document does not re-derive the attribution conventions here (C3, separation artifact §C3 — uniform-site 0.25, uniform-world 0.5333, core-weighted-5× 0.625 at k = 3); it borrows them as an independent, separately verified result.

---

## R3 — The two gates compound

The evidentiary yield of a refuted dated prediction to the core commitment must pass **both** gates:

- **Gate 1 (reach).** Contact probability κ(k; a), a prior quantity, ≤ 0.25 for a ≥ 0.5, k ≥ 2, and 0.0625 at the documented k = 4 with a = 0.5.
- **Gate 2 (localization).** Conditional on contact, the likelihood ratio identifying the core as the fault is exactly 1.0 — no contribution from the observation at all.

Chaining them, the *discriminative* yield of the maximally testable layer to the core is bounded by (reach prior) × (prior attribution share) × (1.0), and the last factor is identically zero in discriminative content. Two independent barriers, both on the prior side of the ledger:

> **R3, the two-gate bound.** No refuted dated prediction can deliver any *observation-driven* update against a core metaphysical commitment. What it delivers is a bookkeeping problem — *which conjunct do you surrender?* — and the answer is selected by prior and convention, never measured by the date's passing.

Three scope caveats, carried from Part 7 without weakening:

1. **"Did not localize" is weaker than "did not lower."** R1–R3 bound the *discriminative* yield, not the magnitude of a possible Bayesian lowering; §7.2 explicitly declines to price P(C | ¬P), and Rowe (1979) / Draper (1989) hold that unpriced catch-all auxiliaries carry a Bayesian cost rather than neutralizing evidence. The burden is symmetric: no fault site is selected by the observation.
2. **The sample is selected.** The three traditions are famous precisely because they survived; no rate of core-abandonment may be read off 3 cases, and the wider literature also documents traditions that did dissolve.
3. **Layer labels are not stable.** The 1844 date was Layer A when predicted; the doctrine built from its failure became Layer C. The A/C classification holds only at the time of prediction.

---

## R4 — What the observed record constrains: a ≈ 0.40

Inverting the R1 table against Part 7's observed tally (0 core contacts in 6 predictions, per-case k = 2, 1, 2) gives the one genuinely *observational* quantity in this artifact: the smallest auxiliary-tenability stipulation consistent with the record at the 5% level, by bisection on *a*.

> **R4.** The observed 0-of-6 record is consistent with auxiliary-move tenability *a* down to approximately **0.40** (below that, seeing 0 contacts in 6 predictions would have probability < 5%). The record therefore does not show "auxiliaries are highly tenable"; it shows that even auxiliaries tenable at only 0.4 — barely better than a coin — are sufficient, at the documented *k* values, to insulate the core in a sample this size. The weaker the stipulated tenability, the more the insulation must come from the *number* of families *k*, which is an observable count.

This is the artifact's own most falsifiable claim, and it is checkable in principle: *k* per case is a matter of record (what reinterpretations the tradition actually used), and *k* = 0 — a refuted prediction with no auxiliary move available — is a real possibility the literature documents elsewhere.

---

## R5 — The N-sensitivity lattice for the C2 threshold

C2's headline (a likelihood ratio of 89,991 per rival) scales with the contested candidate count *N*. The lattice makes the regime-dependence explicit and shows what is invariant:

Required per-rival likelihood ratio *b = (N − 1) · p/(1 − p)*:

| N \ target posterior p | 50% | 90% | 99% |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10² | 99 | 891 | 9,801 |
| 10³ | 999 | 8,991 | 98,901 |
| 4 × 10³ | 3,999 | 35,991 | 395,901 |
| 10⁴ | 9,999 | **89,991** | 989,901 |
| 3.2 × 10⁴ | 31,999 | 287,991 | 3,167,901 |

The **form** *b = (N − 1)·p/(1 − p)* is invariant across the whole contested range of *N*; only the number moves. The structural conclusion — that identifying one tradition among *N* rivals is *N − 1* times harder than answering the binary existence question at the same confidence — holds for every *N* ≥ 11 checked and is not an artifact of choosing 10⁴. Quote the threshold with its *N*; the conclusion does not depend on the choice.

---

## Consolidated quantitative summary

| # | Quantity | Value |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dated predictions examined (Part 7) | 6 |
| 2 | Observed non-occurrences | 6 of 6 |
| 3 | Core contacts (localizations) observed | **0** |
| 4 | Traditions abandoning core | 0 of 3 |
| 5 | Distinct auxiliary-move families documented | 4 |
| 6 | Per-case k (Miller, Martin, Camping) | 2, 1, 2 |
| 7 | κ(1; 0.5) | 0.500 |
